fatal_errors: The hypothesis replaces the target temperature-dependent solid-solution, inertial-dulling, and dynamic-solute-pinning mechanisms with an LCO–stacking-fault-energy–twinning mechanism.
The proposed room-to-moderately-elevated-temperature tensile study omits the cryogenic and high-temperature regimes needed to reveal the target CRSS dulling and Portevin–Le Chatelier effects.
It does not distinguish composition effects on local chemical order from effects on stacking-fault energy, magnetism, elastic properties, or ordinary solid-solution resistance.

The asserted sequence that greater LCO lowers SFE and improves ductility, whereas lower LCO produces higher strength, is not established by the cited evidence and may conflict with evidence that chemical order itself can increase dislocation resistance.
Cost and cost-performance, explicitly requested in the problem, are not incorporated.
explanation: This is a testable and scientifically plausible alternative centered on twinning and metastability, especially for CrCoNi-like compositions, but it is not a reconstruction of the hidden study. The target used [1̄23] single-crystal compression from 9 to 1373 K, strain-rate jumps, TEM, and DFT MSAD to identify three regimes: MSAD-controlled solid-solution strengthening, phonon-drag-controlled inertial dulling below roughly 60–77 K, and Mn/Fe-associated Cottrell-type solute pinning at high temperature. The generated hypothesis instead emphasizes LCO-controlled SFE, twinning, and transformation during tensile deformation. Its falsification rule is reasonably discriminating, although local SFE is largely inferred and correlations could remain confounded. E1, E2, and E4 support the general plausibility of twinning, metastability, and LCO effects, but they do not establish the proposed monotonic causal chain across all 16 alloys; E3 is minimally relevant, and E5 concerns dual-phase HEAs outside the stated single-phase boundary.
